sections.passage: You will hear a conversation between a customer and a travel agent about booking a holiday package to New Zealand. The customer, Mrs. Patricia Hammond, calls Pacific Travel Agency to inquire about a 12-day tour package. She plans to travel with her husband and two children aged 8 and 12 during the summer school holidays in July. The agent, Kevin, explains that they have two main packages: the 'Kiwi Explorer' which covers both North and South Islands, and the 'Southern Adventure' which focuses on the South Island only. Mrs. Hammond is particularly interested in outdoor activities suitable for children, including visits to Hobbiton Movie Set, bungee jumping (for adults only), and the Waitomo Glowworm Caves. Kevin mentions that July is peak winter season in New Zealand, so they should pack warm clothing. The basic package costs $4,200 per adult and $2,800 per child, including flights from London Heathrow with a stopover in Singapore. Accommodation is in 4-star hotels with breakfast included. There is an optional helicopter tour over the Franz Josef Glacier for an additional $350 per person. Mrs. Hammond decides to add the glacier tour and asks about travel insurance, which Kevin says costs $120 per adult and $85 per child for comprehensive cover. They agree that Kevin will send a detailed itinerary by email within 48 hours.

sections.passage: Welcome to Greenfield Health and Wellness Centre. My name is Sarah, and I'll be giving you a brief orientation of our facilities today. We've been serving the local community for over fifteen years, and we recently completed a major renovation costing 2.3 million pounds. The centre is open Monday to Friday from 6 AM until 10 PM, and on weekends from 7 AM until 8 PM. Please note we are closed on public holidays. Our main gymnasium is located on the second floor and features over 150 pieces of state-of-the-art equipment, including a dedicated free weights area, cardio machines with personal screens, and functional training zones. We ask that all members wipe down equipment after use with the disinfectant sprays provided at each station. The swimming pool is 25 metres long and has six lanes. It's heated to 28 degrees Celsius year-round. We offer lane swimming sessions every morning from 6 to 8 AM, after which the pool is open for recreational use. Children under 12 must be accompanied by an adult at all times. Our spa and sauna area is located on the ground floor and is restricted to members aged 16 and over. We have a Finnish sauna, a steam room, and a hot tub. For group fitness classes, we offer over 40 different sessions per week including yoga, Pilates, spinning, Zumba, and aqua aerobics. Classes can be booked online through our app or at reception up to seven days in advance. I'd like to draw your attention to our nutrition counselling service. We have three registered dietitians who offer one-to-one consultations. The initial assessment costs 45 pounds, with follow-up sessions at 30 pounds each. Personal training sessions are also available at 55 pounds per hour, or you can purchase a block of ten sessions for 450 pounds, which represents a saving. For any injuries or physiotherapy needs, we have an on-site clinic open on Tuesdays and Thursdays by appointment. Finally, I should mention our café on the ground floor, which serves healthy meals, smoothies, and snacks. Members receive a 15 percent discount on all food and beverages.

sections.passage: Two business studies students, James and Olivia, are discussing their final-year project with their tutor, Dr. Catherine Williams. Their project examines the impact of social media marketing on small and medium-sized enterprises in the UK retail sector. James explains that they chose this topic because over 78 percent of UK small businesses now use social media platforms for marketing, yet many report difficulty measuring return on investment. Dr. Williams suggests they narrow their focus to a specific platform rather than attempting to cover all social media channels. After discussion, they agree to concentrate on Instagram marketing, as it has shown the highest growth rate among UK retail businesses in the past two years. Olivia has already completed a literature review covering 35 academic sources, including seminal works by Kaplan and Haenlein on social media definitions, and more recent studies by Smith and Zook on digital marketing strategy. Dr. Williams recommends they also look at the Chartered Institute of Marketing's annual reports from 2023 and 2024 for industry data. For their primary research, James and Olivia plan to conduct semi-structured interviews with 20 business owners from three categories: fashion retail, food and beverage, and home and garden. They've designed a questionnaire with 25 questions covering five themes: platform usage patterns, content strategy, budget allocation, customer engagement metrics, and perceived effectiveness. Dr. Williams advises them to pilot test the questionnaire with at least three respondents before full deployment. She also recommends using NVivo software for qualitative data analysis, which is available through the university's site licence at no additional cost. The project deadline is March 15th, with a draft submission expected by February 20th for feedback. Their final report should be between 8,000 and 10,000 words, excluding appendices and references. Dr. Williams emphasizes the importance of including a critical reflection section of at least 800 words, which accounts for 15 percent of the overall mark. She also reminds them that the presentation component, worth 20 percent of the grade, will be scheduled during the first week of April.

title.zh: 第四部分 - 海洋生物学讲座

sections.passage: Today's lecture focuses on coral reef ecosystems and the growing threat of ocean acidification. Coral reefs, often called the rainforests of the sea, cover less than one percent of the ocean floor yet support approximately 25 percent of all known marine species. The Great Barrier Reef off the coast of Queensland, Australia, is the largest living structure on Earth, stretching over 2,300 kilometres and comprising over 2,900 individual reef systems. Ocean acidification occurs when carbon dioxide from the atmosphere dissolves in seawater, forming carbonic acid. Since the beginning of the Industrial Revolution, ocean pH has dropped from approximately 8.2 to 8.1. While this may seem insignificant, the pH scale is logarithmic, meaning this represents a roughly 26 percent increase in acidity. Research conducted by the Australian Institute of Marine Science between 2010 and 2024 has documented a 50 percent decline in coral cover across the northern and central sections of the Great Barrier Reef. The primary mechanism of damage is coral bleaching, which occurs when water temperatures rise by as little as one to two degrees Celsius above the normal summer maximum. During bleaching events, corals expel the symbiotic algae called zooxanthellae that live within their tissues and provide up to 90 percent of the coral's energy through photosynthesis. Without these algae, the coral appears white and, if conditions persist, will die within weeks. However, recent research published in Nature Climate Change in 2024 has identified certain coral species in the Red Sea that demonstrate remarkable thermal tolerance, surviving temperatures up to 5 degrees Celsius above normal bleaching thresholds. Scientists believe these corals have evolved specific heat-shock proteins that protect the zooxanthellae from thermal damage. This discovery has prompted new research into assisted gene flow programmes, where heat-tolerant coral fragments are transplanted to vulnerable reef systems. The economic value of coral reefs is substantial. They generate an estimated 36 billion US dollars annually through tourism, fisheries, and coastal protection. In Australia alone, the Great Barrier Reef supports 64,000 jobs and contributes 6.4 billion Australian dollars to the national economy each year. Marine biologists are now deploying advanced monitoring technologies including autonomous underwater vehicles equipped with hyperspectral cameras that can detect bleaching up to three weeks before it becomes visible to the naked eye. Additionally, machine learning algorithms are being trained on satellite imagery to predict bleaching events with 87 percent accuracy up to four weeks in advance.

title.zh: 文章1 - 制图学的历史

sections.passage:
The art and science of mapmaking, known as cartography, has a history stretching back thousands of years. The earliest known map is a wall painting dated to approximately 6,500 BCE found at Çatalhöyük in modern-day Turkey, depicting a town plan with what appears to be a volcano erupting. However, systematic cartography began with the ancient Babylonians, who created maps on clay tablets as early as 2,300 BCE. The Babylonian World Map, created around 600 BCE, is the earliest known world map, showing Babylon at the centre surrounded by a circular ocean.

The Greeks made significant advances in cartographic theory. Anaximander of Miletus, writing around 550 BCE, was among the first to propose that the Earth was cylindrical in shape and created one of the first maps of the known world. Eratosthenes, the chief librarian at the Library of Alexandria, calculated the circumference of the Earth with remarkable accuracy around 240 BCE, arriving at a figure of approximately 40,000 kilometres — remarkably close to the modern measurement of 40,075 kilometres. Perhaps the most influential figure in ancient cartography was Claudius Ptolemy, a Greco-Egyptian scholar working in Alexandria around 150 CE. His work Geographia contained coordinates for approximately 8,000 locations and introduced the concepts of latitude and longitude that remain fundamental to mapping today.

During the medieval period, European cartography was dominated by mappae mundi — religious world maps that placed Jerusalem at the centre and oriented east at the top. The most famous example is the Hereford Mappa Mundi, created around 1300 CE, which depicts the world as a circle with east at the top and includes detailed illustrations of biblical events, exotic animals, and distant cities. Meanwhile, Islamic cartographers made remarkable progress. Al-Idrisi, working at the court of King Roger II of Sicily, produced the Tabula Rogeriana in 1154, which remained the most accurate world map for three centuries.

The Age of Exploration in the 15th and 16th centuries revolutionised cartography. Gerardus Mercator's 1569 world map introduced the projection that bears his name, which allowed sailors to plot straight-line courses across the oceans. While the Mercator projection distorts the relative size of landmasses near the poles — making Greenland appear roughly the same size as Africa when it is actually fourteen times smaller — it remains the most widely used projection for navigation and online mapping services today.

The 20th century brought aerial photography and satellite technology, transforming mapmaking from a manual to a digital process. The launch of Landsat 1 in 1972 marked the beginning of satellite-based Earth observation. Today, Geographic Information Systems (GIS) integrate multiple data layers to create dynamic, interactive maps used in urban planning, environmental management, and disaster response. The development of GPS technology has democratised navigation, with consumer devices accurate to within a few metres. More recently, collaborative projects like OpenStreetMap have created freely available, crowd-sourced maps that challenge the traditional dominance of government mapping agencies and commercial providers.

sections.passage:
Human decision-making is far more complex and irrational than classical economic theory would suggest. For centuries, economists operated under the assumption of homo economicus — a theoretical human being who makes perfectly rational decisions based on complete information and pure self-interest. However, groundbreaking research by psychologists Daniel Kahneman and Amos Tversky in the 1970s and 1980s fundamentally challenged this view, demonstrating that human decisions are systematically influenced by cognitive biases and mental shortcuts known as heuristics.

Kahneman and Tversky's Prospect Theory, published in 1979, showed that people evaluate gains and losses differently. Specifically, losses loom approximately twice as large as equivalent gains — a phenomenon called loss aversion. In practical terms, losing £100 feels roughly twice as painful as the pleasure gained from finding £100. This asymmetry explains why investors often hold onto losing stocks far longer than rational analysis would recommend, and why people are more motivated to avoid losing what they have than to acquire something new of equal value.

The anchoring effect is another powerful cognitive bias in decision-making. When people are asked to estimate an unknown quantity, their estimates are heavily influenced by any number they have recently encountered, even if that number is entirely irrelevant. In a famous experiment, Kahneman and Tversky spun a wheel of fortune that landed on either 10 or 65, then asked participants to estimate the percentage of African countries in the United Nations. Those who saw the number 10 gave an average estimate of 25 percent, while those who saw 65 estimated an average of 45 percent. This demonstrates how arbitrary reference points can systematically distort our judgements.

The availability heuristic causes people to judge the likelihood of events based on how easily examples come to mind. After highly publicised plane crashes, for instance, many people overestimate the danger of air travel, despite statistics showing it is approximately 100 times safer per kilometre than car travel. Similarly, people tend to overestimate the frequency of dramatic but rare events like shark attacks and terrorist incidents while underestimating common risks like heart disease and diabetes that kill far more people annually.

Confirmation bias — the tendency to search for, interpret, and recall information that confirms one's pre-existing beliefs — pervades nearly every aspect of human reasoning. A 2019 study published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences found that people spend 36 percent more time reading articles that align with their existing views. In the digital age, social media algorithms amplify this tendency by curating content feeds that reinforce users' existing opinions, creating what scholars term 'filter bubbles' or 'echo chambers'.

The framing effect demonstrates that the way information is presented dramatically influences decisions. When a medical treatment was described as having a '90 percent survival rate,' significantly more patients consented than when the same treatment was described as having a '10 percent mortality rate' — despite the information being mathematically identical. This has profound implications for public health communication, insurance marketing, and political messaging.

More recently, researchers have begun exploring how decision-making varies across cultures. A 2022 cross-cultural study involving participants from 23 countries found that collectivist cultures in East Asia showed greater susceptibility to social influence in decision-making, while individualist cultures in Western Europe and North America were more affected by the default effect — the tendency to stick with pre-set options. Understanding these cultural variations is increasingly important as organisations operate across diverse global markets.

title.en: Passage 3 - Urban Planning and Sustainable Cities
title.zh: 文章3 - 城市规划与可持续城市

sections.passage:
The 21st century is the urban century. For the first time in human history, more than half of the world's population lives in cities, and the United Nations projects that by 2050, nearly 70 percent of humanity will be urban dwellers. This unprecedented urbanisation presents enormous challenges for infrastructure, resource management, and quality of life, but also offers remarkable opportunities for sustainable development if cities are planned and managed effectively.

The concept of the '15-minute city', popularised by Paris Mayor Anne Hidalgo and urbanist Carlos Moreno, proposes that all essential services — workplaces, schools, healthcare facilities, shops, parks, and cultural venues — should be reachable within a 15-minute walk or bicycle ride from any resident's home. Paris has begun implementing this vision through its 'Plan Vélo', which has added over 1,000 kilometres of cycling infrastructure since 2020, and through the conversion of school-adjacent streets into pedestrian zones. Barcelona's 'superblocks' programme takes a similar approach, restricting vehicle traffic in clusters of city blocks to create larger pedestrian-friendly neighbourhoods with green spaces, playgrounds, and community areas. Early results from Barcelona show that superblocks have reduced nitrogen dioxide levels by 25 percent and noise pollution by 5 decibels in affected areas.

Singapore, despite its constraints as a small island nation of just 733 square kilometres, has become a global model for urban sustainability. The city-state's 'City in a Garden' initiative has increased green cover from 36 percent in the 1980s to nearly 47 percent today. Buildings like the Khoo Teck Puat Hospital incorporate vertical gardens and rooftop farms, while the iconic Gardens by the Bay complex features supertrees — tree-like structures up to 50 metres tall that collect rainwater, generate solar energy, and serve as air venting ducts for adjacent conservatories. Singapore's NEWater programme recycles treated wastewater into ultra-clean drinking water, meeting up to 40 percent of the nation's water demand, with plans to reach 55 percent by 2060.

Copenhagen in Denmark consistently ranks among the world's most liveable and sustainable cities. The city has committed to becoming carbon neutral by 2025 — the first capital city in the world to set such a target. Key initiatives include a district heating system that serves 98 percent of the city's buildings using waste heat from power plants and biomass facilities, and the CopenHill waste-to-energy plant, designed by architect Bjarke Ingels, which converts waste into energy and features a year-round artificial ski slope and hiking trail on its exterior. Copenhagen's cycling culture is legendary: 62 percent of residents commute to work or school by bicycle, supported by 385 kilometres of dedicated cycling lanes.

However, sustainable urban development faces significant obstacles. Rapid urbanisation in the developing world often outpaces planning capacity. Lagos, Nigeria, for example, has grown from 1.4 million residents in 1970 to over 21 million today, with much of the expansion occurring in unplanned informal settlements lacking basic services. Similarly, Dhaka, Bangladesh, one of the world's most densely populated cities, struggles with chronic flooding, inadequate waste management, and air pollution levels that regularly exceed World Health Organisation safe limits by five to ten times.

Financing remains a critical challenge. The Global Commission on the Economy and Climate estimates that cities need to invest approximately 4.5 trillion US dollars annually in sustainable infrastructure through 2030 to meet climate targets. Innovative financing mechanisms are emerging, including green bonds — fixed-income instruments specifically designated for climate and environmental projects — which grew from 11 billion dollars in 2013 to over 580 billion dollars in 2023. Social impact bonds, where private investors fund public projects and receive returns only if predetermined outcomes are achieved, represent another promising model, though they currently account for a much smaller share of urban investment.

The integration of digital technology into urban management — often termed 'smart city' development — offers additional tools for sustainability. Sensors monitoring air quality, traffic flow, water consumption, and energy use generate real-time data that enables more efficient resource allocation. However, scholars caution that technology alone cannot solve urban challenges. Professor Saskia Sassen of Columbia University argues that truly sustainable cities require 'deep engagement with the social fabric' — ensuring that technological solutions address the needs of all residents, including marginalised communities, rather than simply optimising systems for economic efficiency.

The diagram below shows the process of recycling plastic bottles. Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant. Write at least 150 words.

The recycling process involves seven main stages:
1. Used plastic bottles are collected from households and recycling bins
2. Bottles are sorted by type of plastic (PET, HDPE, PVC) at a materials recovery facility
3. Sorted bottles are compressed into bales and transported to a recycling plant
4. Bottles are thoroughly washed and cleaned to remove labels, adhesives, and contaminants
5. Clean bottles are shredded into small flakes using industrial grinding machines
6. Plastic flakes are melted at temperatures between 200-280°C and reformed into uniform pellets
7. Pellets are sold to manufacturers who use them to produce new products such as clothing fibres, packaging materials, and new bottles

Note: Approximately 58% of plastic bottles are currently recycled in the UK, with the remainder sent to landfill or incineration.
prompt.zh:
下图展示了塑料瓶回收的过程。通过选择和报告主要特征来总结信息，并在相关的地方进行比较。至少写150个单词。

回收过程包括七个主要阶段：
1. 使用过的塑料瓶从家庭和回收箱中收集
2. 在材料回收设施中按塑料类型（PET、HDPE、PVC）分类
3. 分类后的瓶子被压缩成捆并运输到回收工厂
4. 瓶子被彻底清洗以去除标签、粘合剂和污染物
5. 清洁的瓶子使用工业研磨机粉碎成小碎片
6. 塑料碎片在200-280°C的温度下熔化并重新制成均匀的颗粒
7. 颗粒被出售给制造商，用于生产新产品，如服装纤维、包装材料和新瓶子

注：目前英国约58%的塑料瓶被回收利用，其余被送往填埋场或焚烧。
